newsitem.title: USA: Stocks sink for 3rd day on Greenspan talk, bonds unchanged.
newsitem.headline: Stocks sink for 3rd day on Greenspan talk, bonds unchanged.

text.p: Stocks fell for the third day in a row Friday as investors remained cautious after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's warning about lofty stock prices and fuelled speculation about an interest rate hike.
Bond prices were barely changed and the dollar was mixed.
The Dow Jones industrial average closed down 47.33 points at 6,877.74. For the week, the index lost 53.88 points.
In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 1,454 to 1,027 on active volume of 508 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Many technology stocks were under selling pressure, but shares in some key leaders in the sector managed to rally.
But by and large, analysts said the market remained under a pall that was unlikely to lift before Greenspan's second round of testimony next Wednesday to the House of Representatives.

"We'll have to see what happens after everybody absorbs his next comments," said Edgar Peters, chief investment strategist at PanAgora Asset Management Inc. "I think we'll have a lot of sideways volatility for the time being."

For now, analysts said, the wind is clearly out of the stock market's sails, which leaves the sentiment-sensitive sectors like technology that bounded higher in January on heavy fund inflows and high optimism, particularly vulnerable.

On Wednesday, Greenspan rattled the stock market as he spoke in surprisingly blunt terms of his concerns in his semi-annual report on the economy to the Senate, about the risks of inflation as well as the dramatic increase in stock prices.
"I think there's still more to work out for the techs," said Grace Messner, vice president of equity management at Wilmington Trust. "A lot of the stocks are still extremely expensive."
Networking stocks met with another session of stiff selling, as investors reassessed the former high-flying group.
The closely watched 30-year Treasury bond ended unchanged, with a yield of 6.80 percent, as the market braced for next week's U.S. nonfarm payrolls report.

The dollar dipped below the 120 Japanese yen level for the first time in a month, ending the session at 120.23 yen against 120.67 late Thursday. The yen's gains against the German mark helped the dollar edge up to 1.6903 marks against 1.6880 late Thursday.
Coffee prices rose as traders continued to worry about lower supplies this year from Latin America. Most precious metals also rose on concerns about a possible rise in interest rates.

At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, traders shrugged off talk that Brazilian coffee supplies will not be as tight as expected. May futures closed 5.75 cents a pound higher at 176.85 cents, just below the life-of-contract high.
Precious metals ended mostly higher, with COMEX April gold up $4.10 an ounce at $365.10, an eight-week high. May silver closed 6.5 cents an ounce higher at $5.360.
NYMEX April platinum ended up 10 cents at $396.40 but well off the day's highs at $415.00 an ounce. In the physical market, however, platinum was quoted at $398.75 in London, a seven-month high.
NYMEX crude oil prices fell to their lowest level since July as speculators continued to bail out of the market with adequate supplies and mild winter weather sparking the sales.
April crude ended 59 cents lower at $20.30 a barrel, the lowest settlement for spot delivery futures since July 29.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index lost 30.9 points to 4,308.3, capping a fall of 28.5 points since last Friday. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 average lost 464.56 points to 18,557.00, a decline of 2.44 percent. It fell 477.54 for the week.
